progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: bio-m6-b02 (mutagen against mutation; damage is usually repaired; a damaged base becomes a mutation when it is copied before repair; UV is not ionising and joins neighbouring thymines into a dimer that distorts DNA; exposure raises risk, not a guarantee; the five mean counts and the "survival, not mutation" verdict from attempt 11c); bio-m6-b01 (mutation as a lasting change in base sequence that can make a new allele; bacteria and yeast pass it to both daughter cells; the antibiotic dish lets only resistant cells grow, and replica plating copies colonies onto it with a velvet pad); Year 11 Biology (cells divide by mitosis; yeast is a single-celled fungus that reproduces by budding; aseptic technique); chem/bio Working Scientifically (independent, dependent and controlled variables; validity, reliability, accuracy; risk assessments). Not assumed: what a colony represents, relative survival, the difference between time and dose.
progression.startsWith: Compare teacher-prepared yeast colony counts across UV exposure times. The video opens: In the mutagens video, you saw these numbers: a hundred and forty two yeast colonies with no UV, and just five after two minutes. And you saw that fewer colonies doesn't prove more mutants. But why not?
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why each colony grew from a surviving cell or small clump that kept dividing; explaining the four fates of a cell under UV and why mutants are counted among survivors; stating who collects UV data and why (UVC, interlocked cabinet, trained staff); naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables; explaining why the control is handled the same with the lamp off; explaining replicate variation and calculating means; calculating relative survival; graphing means with every plate shown; stating what the data support and what they do not; describing how mutation would be measured; judging validity, reliability and accuracy, including time against dose; writing the risk rows; applying this to a new dataset and to an inoculum flaw. No point-mutation names (bio-m6-b03), no cancer (bio-m6-b05), no survival-curve mathematics.
progression.nextLesson: what one changed base can do to a protein (route entry bio-m6-b03).

teaching.task: After two minutes of UV, a plate of yeast grows five colonies instead of a hundred and forty two. If some cells did mutate, where would they be? What can colony counts tell you about UV exposure, how do you collect and analyse them fairly, and what can't they tell you about mutation?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the b02 numbers and verdict, and the puzzle of why not: where would any mutants be? (1); (2) a colony grows from a surviving cell or small clump that kept dividing, so colony counts estimate survival (2); (3) under UV each cell has one of four fates, and only one leaves no colony (copying stalls at many dimers); mutants are counted as survivors (3); (4) UVC is hazardous, so a teacher collects the data in an interlocked cabinet; students analyse (4); (5) one independent variable, one dependent variable, everything else held the same (5); (6) the control plates are handled the same with the lamp off, so UV is the only difference (6); (7) plates differ because each 100 µL picks up a slightly different number of cells; three plates per time and their mean (7); (8) relative survival compares times on one scale (8); (9) the graph with every plate shows the trend and the spread (9); (10) what the data support (reduced survival under these conditions) and what they do not (mutation) (10); (11) how mutation would be measured: mutants are rare, so millions of exposed cells go on a selective medium; mutant colonies as a fraction of survivors, against unexposed cells, then confirmed (11); validity, reliability, accuracy (12); risk (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the mutagens video showed 142 yeast colonies with no UV and five after two minutes, and that fewer colonies does not mean more mutation, so this data-analysis practical asks where any mutants would be, what colony counts can tell you and what they cannot. A colony grows from a cell that can still divide, so it marks survival; UV gives each cell one of four fates, and only some survivors could carry a mutation. A teacher collects the data in an interlocked cabinet because UVC burns skin and eyes; the fair test changes only exposure time, the zero second control plates go into the cabinet with their lids off and the lamp off, and three plates at each time give means that are turned into relative survival and graphed with every plate shown. The data support reduced survival under these conditions but not mutation, which would need the survivors tested on a selective medium for an inherited trait; validity, reliability and accuracy and the risk assessment follow. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, the second on a plate spread with a tenfold more concentrated suspension.
teaching.openingDecision: In the mutagens video, you saw these numbers: a hundred and forty two yeast colonies with no UV, and just five after two minutes. And you saw that fewer colonies doesn't prove more mutants. But why not? If some cells mutated and survived, where would they be? They'd be hiding inside the colonies that grew. So what can colony counts really tell you?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "In a repeat of this investigation, yeast was spread on agar plates and exposed to UV light in a cabinet at a fixed distance. After incubation, the control plates (0 s) had 145, 151 and 160 colonies. The plates exposed for 45 s had 36, 41 and 46 colonies. Calculate the relative survival of the yeast at 45 s (mean colonies at 45 s as a percentage of the control mean). Show your working." Answer: control mean (145 + 151 + 160) ÷ 3 = 456 ÷ 3 = 152; 45 s mean (36 + 41 + 46) ÷ 3 = 123 ÷ 3 = 41; 41 ÷ 152 × 100 = 27.0 %. Crossed mistake: "73.0 %" (the share that did not form colonies, not the survival). Card defines relative survival as "mean colonies at 45 s as a percentage of the control mean" (learning review M2). (A2) "A student repeated the investigation. To have more colonies to count at 120 s, she spread the 120 s plates with a yeast suspension ten times as concentrated as the one used for all other plates. The control plates (0 s) had a mean of 142 colonies and the 120 s plates had a mean of 52 colonies. She reported a relative survival of 36.6 % at 120 s. Evaluate her result." Answer: not valid as reported: the 120 s plates received ten times as many cells, so two variables changed; 52 colonies correspond to about 5.2 on a standard plate; 5.2 ÷ 142 × 100 = 3.7 %, close to the main data's 3.5 %; correct for the tenfold suspension (5.2 ÷ 142 × 100 ≈ 3.7 %), or use the same suspension for every plate; plating more cells at a high exposure is a valid method when the result is corrected (Revision 2, science check S3). Crossed mistake: "36.6 % survival" (comparing plates given different numbers of cells without correcting for it).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "explain how a range of mutagens operate, including but not limited to:; electromagnetic radiation sources; chemicals; naturally occurring mutagens" this video is a data-analysis practical. Students analyse a teacher-prepared dataset; they do not expose anything to UV. No student is shown operating a UV source, opening an exposed or incubated plate, or standing near a lit lamp; the UV lamp is never shown lit as a safe operating step (route decision, 21 Oct). It teaches: what a colony is and why each colony grew from a surviving cell or small clump that kept dividing; the four fates of a cell under UV (no damage, repaired, too damaged to divide, mutated but alive) and why mutants are counted among the survivors; who collects the data and why (UVC, an interlocked cabinet, trained staff); the fair test (independent, dependent and controlled variables); a control handled the same way as the exposed plates, with the lamp off; replicate plates and their means; relative survival; graphing every plate as well as the means; what the data support and what they do not; how mutation would be measured (test survivors for a new inherited trait, as a fraction of survivors, against the 0 s plates, then confirm it is inherited); validity, reliability and accuracy, including "time is not dose"; the risk assessment (UVC, the biological risk of cultures, ethanol). Placement (Biology playlist order 3): after b01 (order 1) and b02 (order 2), before b03 (order 4, point mutations). So "mutation" means a lasting change in base sequence (b01, b02), the thymine dimer and the repair race are known (b02), and the antibiotic dish and replica plating are known (b01). Point-mutation types are not named (b03). Not re-taught: how UV forms dimers, repair, copying before repair, "mutagen is the cause, mutation is the change", ionising radiation and chemical mutagens (b02, recalled in one clause each); b01's antibiotic dish (recalled in one clause in scene 11, Revision 2; replica plating itself is no longer shown). Not here: cancer and somatic against germ-line effects (b05); point-mutation names (b03); the dose-response mathematics of survival curves (author note f); performing a microbiology plating method (author note b, teacher method only).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: exposure time violet (the independent variable); colony counts and survival amber (the dependent variable); controls green; the 0 s control plates outlined green; "survival" teal and "mutation" terracotta, kept apart wherever both appear; hazards terracotta; grey for tags and callbacks. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. A small grey corner tag stays on every data scene: "teacher-prepared dataset (constructed example)". Reuse: painted plates, inspected 21 Oct on the dark board: `public/assets/biology/y11-budding-yeast-v1.png` (three yeast cells, one budding, 1374 × 1145; scene 2), `m6-agar-dish-top-v1.png` (top-down blank agar plate, 2000 × 2000; scene 2's spread plate and scene 11's selective plate before incubation), `m6-uv-skin-v1.png` (b02's sun and skin block; scene 3 thumbnail only, as the b02 callback). Inspected and not used: `m6-velvet-replica-block-v1.png` (b01's velvet block; dropped in Revision 2 because replica plating one plate cannot detect rare mutants, science check S1); `m6-uv-cabinet-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: its door is open and its lamp glows violet, which would show a lit lamp with an open door; the route decision and the pre-design both rule this out; replaced by the new closed cabinet plate); `m6-antibiotic-colonies-before-v1.png` and `-after-v1.png` (b01's bacterial plates, about 250 and about 15 colonies; their counts do not match this dataset, and reusing an antibiotic plate as yeast would confuse a student who watched b01; fallback only, see Assets); `m7-petri-colonies-v1.png` (mixed moulds and bacteria: wrong organism); `b3a-petri-dish-v1.png` (empty side view; no use here); `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` (owner rule). No human figures.
